# Pyre (gusty repo) — Roadmap tracker

This file is the **tracker**. It is the single source of truth for *what exists*, *what is
next*, and *what is gap-shaped*: every item, gap, status, ADR and piece of evidence is a
row, so state is scannable at a glance and editable one cell at a time.

The **narrative** half — how a gap was found, what the wrong answer looked like, which
measurement settled it, what was rejected — lives in
[`docs/roadmap-details.md`](docs/roadmap-details.md). Each row's `Record` column links
straight to its section, and each row's `Free text` column keeps the item's own sentence
from before the tabulation, so nothing was cut from the roadmap to make it a table: the
wording stayed with the row, the long form moved beside it, and only *statuses* moved into
cells.

> Read `AGENTS.md` first: it fixes the loop, the **one** execution backend (LLVM AOT codegen,
> since ADR 0302 retired the AST interpreter) and the two **witness legs** that evidence a
> compiled answer, and the machine-consumption contract. This file is what the loop reads and
> writes each cycle.

## How to use this file

- **Pick work** from the [Open queue](#open-queue--the-working-list), top row first.
- **Finish work** by changing exactly one cell — the row's `Status` — plus its `Evidence`,
  in the same commit as the code, and appending the story to `docs/roadmap-details.md`.
- **Add work** by appending a row with a fresh, never-reused ID. Never renumber, never
  reuse: comments in `pkg/lang` and the ADRs cite these IDs (`Gap R.33`, `L11.1`, `L11.6`).
- **State lives in cells.** The `Status` cell is the only authority; the `Free text` cell is
  the item's own wording — carried forward verbatim from the pre-tabulation roadmap for rows
  that predate it, and written with the row for rows added since (a Phase 12 row carries its
  three-engine measurement there) — and `Record` links to the full narrative — measurements,
  programs, root causes, rejected alternatives — in `docs/roadmap-details.md`. New prose about
  *why* goes to the record; never write a second status sentence.

### Witness vocabulary (what an evidence cell is claiming since ADR 0302)

There is one runnable backend, so no row in this file — and no comment in a test — may claim that
an answer was "run on two engines". Every behavioural claim is made against one of exactly two
**witness legs**, and the wording has to say which:

| Phrase | Means | Where the witness lives |
|---|---|---|
| **the record leg** | the compiled answer equals the answer the retired AST interpreter recorded for that source | `pkg/lang/testdata/interpreter-golden.json`, read by `pkg/lang/golden.go`; disagreements in `testdata/interpreter-golden-drift.json` |
| **the reference leg** | the compiled answer equals CPython's answer | `gustyc --oracle`, `integration/conformance-matrix.json`; disagreements in `integration/testdata/cpython-debt.json` |
| **both legs** | the compiled answer matches the record *and* CPython | both of the above |

Pre-ADR-0302 wording is **history** and is read through this table rather than rewritten: a row whose
`Free text` says "both legs", "both legs", "the compiled backend" or "interp / aot / python" is
reporting a measurement taken while the record still ran, and its `Path` cell means:
`both` → the compiled backend judged on both legs · `interp` → a claim whose remaining witness is the
record · `aot` → the compiled backend alone. What a row may **not** do is state a present-tense claim
about an engine nobody can start; `pkg/lang/witness_claim_test.go` fails the suite on those, so the
restating happens when a row is touched, not in a single sweep that would quietly rewrite history.

### Status vocabulary (the only markers this file uses)

| Marker | Meaning | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ `DONE` | shipped and verified on every path the item requires | nothing owed; reopening needs a new probe |
| 🟢 `IN PROGRESS` | the active item; steps landed | the row names the next step |
| 🟨 `PARTIAL` | a named subset ships; the remainder is written in the cell | the remainder keeps its own ID where it has one |
| ⏳ `PLANNED` / `OPEN` | not started (planned) or reproduced and unfixed (open) | sits in the queue |
| 🔴 `BLOCKED` | cannot move until the named dependency lands | the cell names dependency + owner |
| 🚫 `NOT A DEFECT` | measured, decided, nothing owed | the cell cites the ADR |

### Column contract

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Path` | `both` = the compiled backend judged on both witness legs (written, before ADR 0302, as "interpreter + LLVM AOT") · `interp` = a claim whose only remaining witness is the record · `aot` = the compiled backend alone · `checker`, `cli`, `tooling`, `docs` |
| `ADR` | decision record in `docs/adr/` (one per feature; `—` when the decision was obvious) |
| `Evidence` | the tests / programs that make the status a measured claim rather than a claim |
| `Free text` | the item's own wording, kept beside the row so the tracker reads on its own: for a row that predates the tabulation, the pre-tabulation roadmap text verbatim (2026-10-01); for a row written since, the text written with it — a Phase 12 row carries its three-engine measurement. Sub-bullets appear as `•`/`↳`, programs as `<code>` blocks, hard-wrapped lines joined. History, not state: where it disagrees with the `Status` cell, the cell is right |
| `Record` | `docs/roadmap-details.md#anchor` — the long form: measurement tables, programs, root cause, alternatives rejected |

The suite is **subprocess-bound** (~6000 toolchain calls for ~3000 cases: `llc` 58 ms, `cc` 13 ms, `lli` 57 ms against 1 ms of Go), so CI runs it through `tools/testshards` — one test process per core, the partition from `go test -list`, measured **10m06s → 3m30s** on four pinned cores — the serial figure is the CI failure, since `go test`'s default is 10m00s (ADR 0313). The **drift ledger is adjudicated once for the run**, over the shards' merged evidence, because a ledger row is a claim about a run and a sharded run is N processes (ADR 0315) | `make test`, `make testshards`, `tools/testshards/main_test.go`, `pkg/lang/golden_evidence_test.go`, L8.2 |
| Toolchain budgets | every external call is bounded — build-stage tools 5m, one oracle run 2m, tunable via `GUSTY_TOOL_TIMEOUT`/`GUSTY_ORACLE_TIMEOUT`; an expired budget is its own class (`*lang.ToolTimeoutError`, **exit 8**, `--json` `phase: "toolchain"`), never filed as a module rejection | `pkg/lang/tool_budget.go`, `pkg/lang/tool_budget_test.go`, `cmd/gustyc/toolchain_timeout_test.go`, ADR 0312 |
| Retired-engine record | 10261 sources with the answer the record holds for each (value, type, stdout, trap class/message, front-end refusal) | `pkg/lang/testdata/interpreter-golden.json`, read by `pkg/lang/golden.go`; the corpus is the retired engine's answers taken at the last commit that had it, and a source first asked after ADR 0302 retired it is recorded from the reference with the compiled leg cross-checked — the file's own `meta` says which is which, and `pkg/lang/golden_artifact_counts_test.go` recomputes the count beside this one (Gap R.204) |
| Rows owed | 244 of 417 queue rows  — the [Open queue](#open-queue--the-working-list) is the only list of owed work | this file |
| Ledgers (two-way ratchets) | 316 + 20 compiled-vs-record divergences (`pkg/lang`, `integration`) · 9 compiled-vs-CPython debts, each naming its owner row | `pkg/lang/testdata/interpreter-golden-drift.json`, `integration/testdata/interpreter-golden-drift.json`, `integration/testdata/cpython-debt.json` |

The ledger behind the oracle column is `integration/conformance_cases.go`: the **absence**
of a row means "this program must behave like CPython", and a `debt` row needs a reason, an
**owner ID from this file**, and a pin per leg. A debt that gets paid fails the build until
the row is deleted — that promotion is the definition of done.

## Open queue — the working list

Top row is next work. `Blocked on` is the only legitimate reason to skip a row, and the
queue order encodes the dependency rules (Phase 11 before the items that read its tag,
Phase 12's silently-wrong rows in the queue's priority-1 class).
Every open row is also pinned in the conformance ledger, so landing it must break a pin.
An item's own wording — including any program listings — is written once, in that item's row
below; the queue points at it by `ID` instead of repeating it.

| Pri | ID | Item | Status | Blocked on | Next concrete action | Definition of done |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

floats (ADR 0238), **nested containers** (ADR 0239), the **tagged element read** (ADR 0241: `xs[0]`, `m[0][1]`, `d["a"][1]`, `t[0][0][0]`, `xs[0] == [1,2]`, `2 in xs[0]`, `len(xs[0])`, `for v in xs[0]`, `y = xs[0][1]`), the **numeric use of an element** (ADR 0243: `xs[0] + 1`, `xs[0] > 2`, `-xs[0]`, `xs[0] / 4`, `xs[0] // 3, xs[0] % 3`, `f(xs[0])`, `d["a"][0] * 2`, `t[0][0] + 1` — answered by both backends, floats taking the float path) and the **numeric use of a slot read through an index the program computes** (ADR 0249: `xs = [10, 4]` / `i = 0` / `print(xs[i] / 4)` → `2.5` where it had exited 2 with `fdiv double , %t1`; A **dict entry and a set member are those positions no longer** (ADR 0310): `print({"k": n})`, `print({n: 1})`, `print({n})` and the bound forms `d = {"k": n}` / `s = {n}` answer what the reference prints, because the entry and the member go to the builders that already take the payload *and* the tag (`rt_dict_put_tagged`, `rt_set_add_tagged`), a register is an `i32`, and a key or member that cannot be hashed raises CPython's `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` from its tag instead of becoming a plausible handle at the exit code of success. What stays open is the same missing word in the positions that keep **one** word for a whole value (the signless call `abs(n)` is **paid — ADR 0309**; **The mutation roads are those positions no longer** (ADR 0311): `xs.append(n)`, `s.add(n)`, `xs[i] = n` and `d[k] = n` answer what the reference prints, each going to the door that takes payload and tag together (`rt_append_tagged`, `rt_set_add_tagged`, `rt_put_elem`+`rt_tag_elem`, `rt_dict_put_tagged`), with the container promoted to describing its slots and an unhashable pair key or member raising CPython's own sentence. What the row still owes is `min(n, 3)`, a literal `sum`/`min`/`max` folds into a static array, a pair handed across a call, a value that is not a pair written into a slot (`d["k"] = xs[0] / 2`), and the call's own answer read as one number — Gap R.146), a pair parameter beside an ordinary one (Gap R.154), a tuple-unpacking target (Gap R.144), and the membership test and the loop over **the container the program built** — the first slot deep is **paid by ADR 0323** (Gap R.95: `7 in xs[0]` is `True`, `"k" in d["a"]` asks a dict's keys, `for v in xs[0]` prints `7`/`8`, and a slot holding a number raises the reference's own sentence with the two wordings the two questions use), — and the **second slot deep is paid the same way** (ADR 0324, closing Gap R.210: `7 in xs[0][0]` is `True`, `for v in d["a"]["k"]` prints `1`/`2`, a chain four long steps and tests, because `builtSlotPair` hands the pair ADR 0251's recursive read computes to the same four arms), **with the needle read the way the haystack is** (ADR 0324, closing Gap R.211: a container read out of one slot is found inside another by content, and a container needle into a dict or a set slot raises `unhashable type: 'list'` from the needle's tag rather than answering "not present") — leaving a needle whose kind cannot be proven as Gap R.212 beside Gap R.83's unprovable comparison operand, and **the kind an instance slot carries paid by ADR 0325** (Gap R.209: `xs.append(C())` / `print(xs[0])` is `<__main__.C object at 0x…>` rather than the heap handle, `len(xs[0])` / `1 in xs[0]` / `for v in xs[0]` name `C`, and a text haystack asked about an instance raises the reference's `'in <string>' requires string as left operand, not C`); the pair-bound name read back as one static number (`print(n + 1)`, `-n`, `if n:`, an f-string, `n += 1`) is paid (ADR 0268, Gap R.143). **The two operators that choose an operand answer the operand** (ADR 0269, closing Gap R.147): `print(2 and 3)` is `3`, `print(0 or 5)` is `5`, `print("" or "d")` is the text `d`, `print([1] and [2])` is `[2]` and the pair that proves the rule — `print(True or 1)` is `True` beside `print(1 or True)` is `1` — on both engines, where both had printed `1` at exit 0; a *condition* still composes the two operands' truths (`truth(a and b)` is `truth(a) and truth(b)`, so `if x or "d":` branches on operands that share no word), a value position picks its operand with one `select` in the `i32` or the `double` word, and the print door selects the payload **and** the tag for the module's one tag-reading printer — which is why `print(x or "d")` prints a word and not an `@str_tab` index. A shape none of those roads can state refuses by naming both operands and the missing tag rather than answering `1`, and the checker types the expression by its operand instead of by a bool the operator never returns. **The same two operators skip the operand the test rejected** (ADR 0275, closing Gap R.149): `print(x and boom())` with x bound to 0 is silent, `print(x and (1 // 0))` answers `0` where both engines raised `ZeroDivisionError`, `if x and boom():` never calls `boom`, `while x and boom():` never enters, and the operand the test *does* reach runs exactly once — `print(boom() and 2)` used to call `boom` twice compiled, once from the generic operand lowering and once from the door that selected. The four doors (`logicCondition`, `logicValue`, `logicDouble`, `logicPrintPair`) now emit one skeleton — left operand once, `br i1` on its truth, the right operand only in the block the branch enters, one `phi` per arm (a second beside it when the answer is a pair), and `@rt_pair_truth` asked which arm a tagged operand is; the `select`-based `logicSelectPair` left the module with the second evaluation it could not avoid. **The negation of anything without a sign is paid** (ADR 0266, closing Gaps R.89 and R.137): `-"hi"`, `-None`, `-[1, 2]`, `-{"a": 1}`, `-Token()`, `-xs[0]` over a container the literal says holds no number, and the same operand inside a float expression each raise CPython's own `bad operand type for unary -: '<kind>'` on **both** engines — the interpreter asks the value, the module asks the expression, the constant folders decline the shape, and `except TypeError:` reaches every one of them; `-[1, 2]` had been `%t1 = sub i32 0, @.lst1` and **exit 2**. **True division was the exception and is paid** (ADR 0253, closing Gap R.96): `xs = []` / `xs.append(3)` / `print(xs[0] / 4)` answered `0.0` with exit 0 — ADR 0249's empty-operand `fdiv` substituted into silence — and answers `0.75` on both engines now, because `/` is a float whatever arrives, so the tag decides whether to unbox (`rt_float_of`), to convert (`sitofp`, int or bool) or to raise CPython's `unsupported operand type(s) for /` sentence per kind, with the zero guard inside each arm so the wording (`division by zero` / `float division by zero`) is the one the program's `except` matches; and an operand that still cannot be lifted is refused rather than substituted, with `fdiv/fadd/fmul/fsub double ,` blacklisted module-wide. Beside it, a comparison with an expression whose kind cannot be proven (Gap R.83: `xs[0] == pick(1)`, where `pick` returns text on one path and a number on another — a wrong answer until ADR 0247, a refusal for `==` and since ADR 0252 a measured verdict for `>`), and the ordering of two built slots by their payloads (Gap R.97). | 1a | Gap R.242 | **`a-b` is not a subtraction — the lexer's `-1` rule eats the operator**: `x = 5` / `y = x-1` / `print(y)` writes **`5`** where the reference writes `4`, at **exit 0**. The subtraction was not mis-evaluated, it was never parsed: `pkg/lang/lexer.go`'s `case c == '-' && i+1 < n && unicode.IsDigit(rune(src[i+1]))` emits `-1` as a single `TokInt` whenever a minus is directly followed by a digit, whatever token came before it, so the program becomes `y = x` followed by an expression statement `-1`, and the answer is the value the subtraction never produced. The same tokens in an expression position are refused instead: `print(1-1)` dies with `parse error at 1:8: expected ")"`, and with it `print(x-1)`, `print(len(xs)-1)`, `print(xs[2-1])`, `print(3.5-1)`, `for i in range(3-1):` — one defect, two faces, the silent one and the refused one. Write the same expression with a space (`x - 1`) and it answers correctly, which is the only reason a suite written in this house's style has never seen it; it is the priority-1 class (a wrong value at the code that means the program ran) on the most ordinary arithmetic in the language. Measured 2026-10-14 while landing ADR 0337 | ✅ `DONE` — closed 2026-10-14 by **ADR 0338**: the `-` before a digit is asked what it FOLLOWS — one token of context, asked where the token is cut. `minusBeginsLiteral` reads the last emitted token (skipping a homoglyph `TokWarning`, which is not a token of the program at all): after a number, a name, any of the five text forms, a closing `)` `]` `}`, or one of `True`/`False`/`None`, the minus is the SUBTRACTION operator and the parser's existing unary-minus rule takes whatever comes next; everywhere else — start of a line, after an operator, after `,` `:` `(` `[` `{` `=`, after `return`/`in`/`else`/`not` — `-N` stays ONE literal, which is what keeps `print(-1)`, `print(-1.5)`, `xs[-1]`, `[1,2,3][-1]`, `{-1: "n"}`, `f(-1)`, `2 ** -1`, `def f(a=-1)` and `xs[-1] = 9` answering exactly as they did. The three literal keywords end an expression and every other keyword begins a position, which is the difference between `print(True-1)` answering `0` and answering a stray `-1`; `-=` is untouched (longest match, so `x -= 1` is still one token and `x-=-1` is `-=` followed by `-1`), and a `-` inside a text or a comment is not a token at all | ADR 0166 (the refused face was a parse error at exit 1, and a refusal is the wrong answer to a program the reference runs), ADR 0249 (the two refusals this row leaves standing name what is missing), ADR 0273 (the rule reads a token, emits nothing, advances no counter), ADR 0302 (the newly answered sources are recorded from the reference, not self-certified), L11.1 (owns the static-list comprehension this row leaves refused; ## Phase tables

<details>
<summary>Original section text, verbatim (New work — modern 2026 language-design roadmap)</summary>

These are *new* phases layered on top of the existing DONE work. Each item is a first-class roadmap entry with an ADR, a unit test, and an `integration/` program where relevant. Order reflects dependency: front-end (lexer/parser) first, then semantics/type system, then runtime, then codegen, then tooling.

</details>

A row's `Status` states whether **that row's** Definition of Done is met (see the two DoD
sections at the bottom). An open follow-on is named inside the cell and carried exactly
once in the [queue](#open-queue--the-working-list) above.

### Phase 4 — lexer modernization

<details>
<summary>Original section text, verbatim (Phase 4 — lexer modernization (2026))</summary>

**Goal: a resilient, position-rich lexer that supports a modern source surface.**

</details>

| ID | Item | Status | Path | ADR | Evidence | Free text (verbatim from the pre-tabulation record — the Status column is the authority) | Record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L4.1 | Error-recovering lexer: `TokError` + resume, several diagnostics per run, parse-partial still checked | ✅ `DONE` | both | 0177 | `lexer_test.go`, `check_test.go` | Error-recovering lexer — on an unexpected character, emit a `TokError` token carrying the span + message and *resume*, instead of aborting the whole file. The parser/semantic can then report multiple diagnostics per run (feed the LSP). ✅ DONE (ADR 0177) — the lexer recovers (`emitErr` appends a `TokError` and keeps scanning) and the parser reports a `ParseErrors` forest, but the last hop was discarding both: `CheckSource` / `CheckFile` returned a Go error, which threw away `prog.Diags` (the precise `unexpected character "$"` spans), collapsed the forest into one `Error()` string, skipped `Analyze` — so type errors in statements that *had* parsed went unreported — and left `--json check` printing prose. A failed parse is now data: one `Diagnostic` per recovered error with the stable `parse.error` code, sorted into document order, and the statements that parsed are still checked. One run on a file with two bad lines yields all three diagnostics in both shapes. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l4-1) |
| L4.2 | Rich token spans (byte **and** rune offsets, multi-line flag) | ✅ `DONE` | both | — | probed not assumed: a triple-quoted token reports its rune range | Rich token spans — each token carries `start` AND `end` (byte + rune offsets), plus an optional multi-line flag, so f-strings, slices, and `match` patterns have exact ranges for hover/diagnostics/formatting. ✅ DONE — verified against the code (probed, not assumed): `Token` carries `Start`/`End` byte offsets and `StartRune`/`EndRune` rune offsets plus `Multiline`, and a triple-quoted string token reports `multiline=true` with exact rune ranges. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l4-2) |
| L4.3 | Unicode identifiers (`ID_Start`/`ID_Continue`, NFC, homoglyph warning) | ✅ `DONE` | both | 0155 | `lexer_test.go` (`café`, `Ο` vs `O`) | Unicode identifiers — accept the full `XID_Start`/`XID_Continue` classes (not just ASCII), with NFC normalization + a clear diagnostic for confusables (e.g. `l` vs `1`, `Ο` vs `O`). ✅ DONE — lexer now decodes UTF-8 runes and scans identifiers by Unicode `ID_Start`/`ID_Continue` categories (letters + Nl + Other_ID_Start additions for start; plus marks, digits, connector punctuation, and Other_ID_Continue for continuation), NFC-normalizes identifier text via `golang.org/x/text/unicode/norm` (so decomposed and precomposed spellings are one symbol), and emits a `TokWarning` → `LevelWarning` diagnostic for Greek/Cyrillic homoglyph lookalikes (e.g. `Ο` U+039F vs Latin `O`). ASCII-start identifiers may continue through multi-byte runes (e.g. `café`). <summary>Original section text, verbatim (Phase 7 — runtime: concurrency, effects, precise GC (2026))</summary>

**Goal: a deterministic async core + memory-safety hardening.**

| ID | Item | Status | Path | ADR | Evidence | Free text (verbatim from the pre-tabulation record — the Status column is the authority) | Record |

| L7.1 | Async runtime: `async def` returns a coroutine object, `await` runs it to completion, `async for` awaits each element | ✅ `DONE` — mid-body suspension and `__aenter__`/`__aexit__` are future work (→ L7.6a) | interp (AOT stays eager) | 0195 | `async_test.go`, `effects_test.go`, `probe_async_eager` | Async runtime (`async`/`await`) ✅ DONE — cooperative async in the interpreter: `async def` returns a *coroutine object* (deferred thunk; the body does not run at call time), `await` runs it to completion (deterministic, race-free), and `async for` awaits each coroutine element. AOT keeps eager semantics; parity holds because awaited async calls run once to completion in both backends (codegen `await` evaluates its operand). `async with` remains eager (`__enter__`/`__exit__`); mid-body suspension and `__aenter__`/`__aexit__` protocols are future work. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l7-1) |
| L7.2 | Precise stack roots: interpreter frame set + watermark; AOT root stack (`@gc.roots`, `rt_root_put`, `rt_frame_open/close`) | ✅ `DONE` | both | 0181 | `gc_roots_ir_test.go`, `gc_stress_test.go`, `gc_precise.gy`, `GUSTY_GC_STRESS=1` | Precise stack roots — replace conservative mark-and-sweep with precise rooting: the GC knows exactly which stack slots/registers hold handles (fixes Gap A's instance-layout bug at the root cause). ✅ **DONE (this round, ADR 0181)** — both backends. *Interpreter*: the root set is `Vars` ∪ active call frames ∪ declared root groups ∪ permanent roots; a watermark makes everything allocated after the last safe point unconditionally live; safe points are statement boundaries with an empty expression stack, plus the body of a *statement-root* call. Collection now actually runs while programs execute (it used to be reachable only from tests), a loop's garbage is reclaimed, a 2000-input REPL session stays bounded, and `GUSTY_GC_STRESS=1` + `integration/gc_stress_test.go` stress the whole corpus under a collection at every statement. Stubbing `pushFrame` makes `TestGCFramesKeepRecursionLive` fail with `cannot index null`. *Compiled backend*: the static per-(scope,name) root table became a **root stack** — `@gc.roots` + `@gc.kinds`, `rt_root_put`/`rt_root_clear`/`rt_frame_open`/ `rt_frame_close`; prologues open a frame, every handle store pushes (deduped per frame), scalar stores tag the entry dead, every return and unwind edge pops, and `rt_gc` traces only tagged entries while counting what it skipped. Fixing it exposed two latent codegen faults it now depends on: a variable's slot must be allocated once per call (`hoistAllocas` — an `alloca` left in a loop body changed address every iteration: `top` hit 2002, the 1024-slot heap filled, the program died), and every function-emitting path including `emitClassMethod` must pop what it pushed. The instance-layout bug that Gap A worked around is rooted out at the cause. *Machine path*: `GCStats`, `--gc-stats` (either backend, stderr), the `gc` member of `--json`, `definitions.gcStats` (incl. `top`) in `--schema`, and `lang.ParseGCStatsLine` ↔ `GCStats.String` round-trip. `gc_precise.gy` is in the conformance matrix; the AOT half is pinned by structural invariants (`pkg/lang/gc_roots_ir_test.go`) and by runtime assertions calibrated against stubs (no frame pop → "19 objects still live"; no hoisting → "root stack grew to 1210"). | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l7-2) |

| L7.4 | Refcount + cycle-collect hybrid | ⏳ `PLANNED` | both | — | — | Refcount + cycle-collect hybrid — refcount for acyclic data (fast reclaim), tracing collector for cycles; deterministic pause for the AOT path. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l7-4) |
| L7.5 | Algebraic effects: one lowering for `raise` / `yield` / `await` | ⏳ `PLANNED` | both | — | — | Algebraic effects — a `raise`/`yield`/`await` effect system as a first-class control-flow model in codegen, unifying exceptions, generators, and async (one lowering, one runtime). | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l7-5) |
| L7.6 | Effect / async exhaustiveness as a semantic check (`async.coro.*`, `async.await.*`, `--effects`) | ✅ `DONE` | checker | 0195 | `effects_test.go` (unit + integration) | Effect/async exhaustiveness ✅ DONE — the await/return discipline is a semantic check, not a runtime promise: `async.coro.never_awaited`, `async.coro.awaited_twice` and `async.generator.unsupported` refuse programs whose async meaning is broken, `async.await.outside_coroutine`, `async.async_stmt.outside_coroutine`, `async.await.not_coroutine` and `async.missing_return` warn where the program still means something. The proof (effect signatures + a flow-sensitive coroutine-liveness walk) is shared by the checker and the codegen and machine-readable: `gustyc --effects` (ADR 0195). See Gap R. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l7-6) |

The report is read back from the artifact: `gustyc --debug-info <src>` (`definitions.debugInfo`, per-function coverage, IR-line-to-source-line rows, a `defect` field when module and emitter disagree) and `--build --debug`'s `dwarf` member (`definitions.dwarfReport`), produced by `llvm-dwarfdump --debug_line` over the linked object — `skipped` for a missing toolchain, never `ok`. Honoured by `--build`, `--emit-llvm` and `--jit/--aot`; source map v2 carries the same table. ### Phase 11 — one tagged value model

<details>
<summary>Original section text, verbatim (Phase 11 — one tagged value model: nested data, real tuples, code-point strings (2026))</summary>

**Goal: a *value* is one thing everywhere.** Every divergence still found by probing against CPython, and every remaining invalid-module / crash / "unsupported" defect in the compiled backend, has the same root: an AOT value is an **untagged `i32`** — a handle, an interned string index, or a compile-time global name — so it cannot say *what it is*. It cannot nest, it cannot mix kinds, it cannot carry `True` vs `1`, and the moment the compiler must decide, it either guesses (wrong answer) or refuses (an `llc` rejection the exit-code contract then blames on the compiler). Phase 11 fixes the representation **once**, and absorbs the representation-shaped half of Gaps J.2, J.6, L.2, N.2, P.1 and P.2 instead of patching each symptom.<br>**Why now (measured, `gustyc` at `b704a14`, corpus green).** Parity compares the backends to *each other*; the CPython oracle exists in only two files (`integration/escapes_test.go`, `integration/division_test.go`), so a construct *both* backends get wrong is invisible to CI. Each row below was run through `--interp`, `--aot` and `python3` on the same source, today:

| program | CPython | `--interp` | `--aot` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `print(True)` | `True` | `1` | `1` |
| `print([1, "a"])` | `[1, 'a']` | `[1, 'a']` ✅ | refused (Gap J.6 diagnostic) |
| `m = [[1,2],[3,4]]` / `print(m[0][1])` | `2` | `2` | `index requires an inline list/dict/set literal` |
| `d = {"a": [1,2]}` / `print(d["a"][1])` | `2` | `2` | same refusal |
| `xs = []` / `xs.append([1,2])` | ok | ok | **invalid IR**: `call void @rt_append(i32 %h2, i32 @.lst1)` |
| `sa = {x for x in [3,1,2]}` | `{1, 2, 3}` | `{3, 1, 2}` | **invalid IR**: `store i32 @.set1, i32* %_sa` (Gap J.2) |
| `print(sorted([3,1,2]))` | `[1, 2, 3]` | ✅ | **invalid IR**: `printf(... , i32 @.lst1)` |
| `t = (1,2,3)` / `print(t[1]); print(t)` | `2` / `(1, 2, 3)` | `2` / `[1, 2, 3]` | `unsupported expression *lang.Tuple` |
| `xs = [1,2,3]` / `print(xs[-1])` | `3` | `IndexError` | `IndexError` |
| `print([1,2,3][-1])` | `3` | `IndexError` | **Go panic** in `irGen.value` (`codegen.go:4314`) |
| `print("abc"[-1])` | `c` | `IndexError` | `string index out of range` |
| `len("café")` / `"héllo"[1]` | `4` / `é` | `5` / `195` | `5` / `195` (Gap N.2) |
| `for c in "aé": print(c)` | `a`,`é` | ✅ | **invalid IR**: `store i32 @.str1, i32* %_c` |
| `def f(x): return x*2` / `print(f(0.1))` | `0.2` | `0.2` | `0` (Gap P.1) |
| `print(-7 // 2)` / `x=8; x/=2; print(x)` | `-4` / `4.0` | ✅ | `-3` / `4` (Gap P.1) |
| `print(-3.5 % 2.0)` | `0.5` | `-1.5` | `-1.5` (Gap P.2 — **both** backends) |
| `import math; print(math.PI)` | `3.141592653589793` | ✅ | `3` (stdlib constants fold to int) |
| `def apply(f, xs): … f(x)` | works | works | `unsupported call "f"` (ADR 0161 note) |
| `class B(A)` / `A.__init__(self, x)` | `3` | `3` | **SIGSEGV** in the JIT (cgo) |
| `def m(self): return "hi"` (called) | `hi` | `hi` | **invalid IR**: `ret i32 @.str1` |

**Items (each: ADR + unit test + `integration/` program, per the Definition of done).** L11.9 is ✅ DONE (ADR 0186) — its 16 probe programs are the measured form of every row below, so an item is not done until its probe's pins change. Order is dependency order — L11.1 is the keystone; do not start L11.3/L11.4/L11.5 before it, or they re-decide the representation locally.

An untagged `i32` cannot say what it is, so it cannot nest, cannot mix kinds, and cannot
carry `True` vs `1`: every remaining invalid-module, crash or "unsupported" defect has that
one root. Do not start L11.3 / L11.5 / L11.6 before L11.1 — they would re-decide the
representation locally. The measured divergence table that motivated the phase is in the
[record](docs/roadmap-details.md#phase-11); the live state of each of its rows is the pin in
`integration/conformance_cases.go`, not a paragraph here.

| ID | Item | Status | Path | ADR | Evidence | Free text (verbatim from the pre-tabulation record — the Status column is the authority) | Record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L11.1 | Tagged value word — one tag table, then tags on every element path | 🟢 `IN PROGRESS` — **landed:** one tag table + heap-kind projection (0182), a tag per element (0184), mixed-list loops bind `(value, tag)` (0185), payload+tag written and read as pairs (0187), containers compare by value (0189), mixed dicts/sets + tagged lookup + promotion (0232). **Open:** nested containers (element handles are not marked by the collector), floats in containers (`rt_print_mixed_value` has no float branch), `@estr[h]` retirement, bools as values — **the print half paid by ADR 0257** (one shared AST question, `IsBoolExpr`, decides how a value is written, so `print(True)`, `print(1 == 1)`, `str(True)`, an f-string and `--json` all say `True`/`bool` on both backends), leaving the one shape where a tag has to travel: a bool through a call (Gap R.111) — **and the container element tag paid by ADR 0259** (Gap R.112: `print([True, 1])` is `[True, 1]`, `print({"k": True})` is `{'k': True}`, `print({True, 1})` is `{True}`, the tag asked in one place instead of three transcribed lists, and every numeric, ordering, equality and membership question about the same slot still answered by its number; and the FOLD door — `@rt_pair_fold` picks the winner of a fold the compiler cannot settle and writes its payload beside its tag, `sum` folding with `@rt_num_arith`'s `+` so the cross-kind sentence is the operator's own (ADR 0316)) | both | 0182, 0184, 0185, 0187, 0188, 0189, 0232 | `value_tags_test.go`, `heapargs_test.go`, `mixed_list_test.go`, `mixed_dict_set_test.go`, `container_eq_test.go`, `container_element_test.go`, `mixed_container_test.go`, `string_containers_test.go`, `bool_element_test.go`, `render_pair_test.go`, `mixed_element_reads.gy`, `mixed_element_writes.gy`, `container_equality.gy`, `probe_bool_in_a_container.gy` | Tagged value word (both backends) 🟢 IN PROGRESS — one value shape on both sides: the interpreter's `value.go` tag set and a compiled `rt_value` (`{i64 payload, i64 tag}`, or a boxed slot with a parallel tag word) become the *same* enum, generated from one table so the two cannot drift (mirror the single-source-of-truth rule of `predeclared.go` / `exceptions.go`). Containers store tagged words, not bare handles ⇒ **per-element tagging** falls out: heterogeneous `[1, "a"]`, nested `[[1,2],[3,4]]`, `d["a"][1]`, `xs.append([1,2])`, `{'k': True}` all lower, print, index and iterate. The compile-time element-kind maps (`listElemStr`/`listElemInt`/`setElem*`/ `dictKey*`/`dictVal*`, ADR 0175) become a *property of the object* read from the tag, so the ADR 0175 refusal retires and the `@estr[h]` per-object flags (ADR 0174) collapse into the tag. Kills the whole `store i32 @.strN` / `ret i32 @.str1` / `rt_append(i32, i32 @.lstN)` / `store i32 @.setN` invalid-IR family at the source. DoD: `programs/nested_data.gy (planned)` + `programs/probe_heterogeneous.gy` byte-identical on both backends *and* equal to CPython; no `i32 @\.(str\|lst\|dict\|set)` ever appears in an argument or store position (extend `runtime_ir_test.go` to assert it module-wide). Pairs with L7.2/L7.3 — a tag is what makes precise rooting and NaN-boxing well-defined.<br>↳ ✅ **Done (ADR 0182): one tag table, and the compiled heap's kind is a projection of it.** Three vocabularies answered "what kind is this": `ValueTag` (`value.go`, read by the interpreter's heap, the compiled `%obj` values and `rt_obj_is`), the ABI tags (`abi.go`, the exported ABI), and the heap's `kind` word (`heapargs.go`, `rt_alloc`'s parameter and the collector's dispatch) — where a list was `5` in one and `1` in the other, written into IR as a literal `rt_alloc(i32 1)` at a dozen sites. Now `heapKindOrder` is the projection (`none=0, list=1, dict=2, set=3, instance=4`), `HeapKindFor`/`HeapTagFor` translate both ways, names come from `kindForTag` (so `HeapKindName` no longer spells them out a second time), codegen allocates through named constants, and `gustyc --lang` prints both tables with `definitions.valueTag` in `--schema`. Verified against stubs: renumbering `HeapKindSet` fails with "codegen allocated an unknown heap kind 5", and swapping the projection order fails the round-trip test.<br>↳ ✅ **Done (ADR 0184): a tag word per element.** `@heap_tags : [1024 x [256 x i32]]` sits parallel to the element slots (a fourth struct field would have rewritten every existing GEP in the same commit that changes behaviour) and carries the canonical `ValueTag` numbers, so `int=0` is both the zero value and "integer" with no init pass. `rt_print_list_mixed` is `rt_print_list` with the container-wide `@estr[h]` load replaced by a per-slot tag load. `xs = [1, "a", None, 2]` now compiles and prints `[1, 'a', None, 2]` — identical to CPython and to the interpreter — where ADR 0175 refused it. `elemKindTag` is the gate: numbers, interned strings and `None` only; **bools** (not values yet), **floats** (the mixed printer has no float rendering) and **containers** (the collector cannot mark elements) stay refused, as does anything whose string-ness codegen cannot prove, because printing a string table *index* as a number is the very bug the original refusal prevented. Loop bodies (`for i in range(N): xs = [i, "a", None]`), string variables, last-assignment-wins rebinding and string-returning calls all work; a 150-iteration loop is tested to actually collect (`freed=148`) while printing correctly. `integration/string_containers_test.go`'s "must be refused" rows for literals moved to a print-correctly test in this commit.<br>↳ ✅ **Done (ADR 0185): `for x in xs` over a mixed list.** The loop already computes the index, so the tag is available where the value is bound: the runtime list loop fetches `rt_get_elem(h, i)` *and* `rt_tag_of(h, i)` into `%_x` / `%_x_tag`, and `print(x)` dispatches on the tag at run time. `rt_print_mixed_value` gained a `quote` flag — container printing passes 1 (`repr()`, quoted, from the interned repr slot of ADR 0174), top-level printing passes 0 (`str()`) — which is Gap L.2's str/repr split landing where it can be implemented. Anything else with the variable refuses via one guard in `value()`: "print(x) works, but using it as a number needs a tagged value". Stub check: pinning the tag to 0 prints `1\n0\n0` and fails the parity rows.<br>↳ ✅ **Done (ADR 0187): element reads and writes carry the tag.** The CPython oracle found the first of these as a *wrong answer in a passing build*: `xs[0] = "z"` on a mixed list stored the payload through `rt_put_elem` and never wrote `@heap_tags`, so `print(xs)` answered `[1, 'a', None]` — the interned index of `"z"`, rendered through the slot's stale `int` tag. Both backends agreed, so the two-backend matrix had nothing to say. The rule now: **the operation that writes a slot's payload writes its tag**. `rt_append_tagged(h, v, t)` appends both in one call (the tag array is not cleared on free, so a forgotten tag reads back the previous tenant's tag); item assignment emits `rt_put_elem` + `rt_tag_elem` inside the same bounds-checked block and skips the container-wide kind bookkeeping, because the tags carry the truth. Reading emits `rt_get_elem` + `rt_tag_of`, and two uses of the pair are open: `print(xs[i])` dispatches on the tag, and `v = xs[i]` binds a tagged variable (the same `%_v`/`%_v_tag` pair ADR 0185 gives a loop variable, so `print(v)` and rebinding-to-retire-the-tag came free). Payload and tag are cross-checked — one saying interned-string while the other says number refuses rather than emitting IR. Still refused, with a message naming what works: arithmetic, comparison, call arguments and format specs on a tagged element, dict/set key reads, and elements the tag cannot describe (bool, float, nested container). New parity programs `mixed_element_reads.gy`, `mixed_element_writes.gy`; two older tests that asserted `print(xs[i])` *must* refuse were inverted, and every refusal test now asserts the refusal's text so a future opening is noticed.<br>↳ ✅ **Done (ADR 0189): containers compare by value.** `xs == ys` for two equal lists answered False on *both* backends — the comparison compared heap handles — and the bug went the other way too: a stored string is an index into `@str_tab`, so `[0] == ["zero"]` was **True**, the interned index matching the number. `if [1] == 1:` emitted `icmp eq i32 @.lst1, 1` and llc refused the module; in the interpreter `!=` was not even the negation of `==`, so `[1] == [1]` and `[1] != [1]` both answered False. Now `rt_container_eq` walks the containers the way Python's `__eq__` does — lists positional, sets and dicts by containment (a positional walk would make `{1, 2} == {2, 1}` False) — and every element is the `(payload, tag)` pair, compared by `rt_slot_eq`. The tag is what makes that sound: without it the payload collision returns. **Stub check**: delete the builder tag stores and `TestTaggedElementsDistinguishPayloadCollisions` answers True where CPython answers False. Following ADR 0187's pairing rule to its end found four builders that had never written tags — the plain list/dict/set literal builders, the container-variable assignment builders, and `heapArg`, which hand-rolled its own `rt_alloc` + `rt_dict_put` loop for call arguments. An untagged slot is uninitialised memory: a container could compare unequal to an *identical* container depending on which heap slot it landed on. `heapArg` now delegates to `heapSetFrom`/`heapDictFrom`, so a container is built in exactly one place per kind; mutation uses `rt_append_tagged` / `rt_set_add_tagged` / `rt_dict_put_tagged` (whose update path also rewrites the value's tag). `Tripwire`: `TestEveryContainerBuilderWritesTags` covers ten build paths. Container-vs-proven-scalar is decided statically (with both operands still evaluated so side effects survive); container-vs-*unknown* refuses — "comparing a container with X needs a tagged value" — which is L11.2 named precisely. `is` stays identity, and `!=` is `==`'s negation. New parity program `programs/container_equality.gy`, which reports verdicts through `if` so the row tests equality and not the bool-rendering debt `probe_bool_value` pins. **Latent, and now closed (ADR 0232)**: dict key lookup and set dedup compared payloads only, so they became unsound the moment a string and a number could collide — L11.1 (1b) carried the tag into `rt_dict_get`/`rt_dict_has`/`rt_set_add`/`rt_contains`, not only into equality.<br>↳ ✅ **Done (ADR 0232): mixed dicts and sets, and the lookup that reads the tag.** The compiled path refused `{"a": 1, "b": "x"}` and `{1, "a"}` outright ("either strings or numbers, not both"), and — the part that mattered more — answered questions wrongly for the containers it *did* accept. Strings are `@str_tab` indices, so an interned string and an integer of the same number are the same bits: `d = {1: "one"}; print(d["a"])` answered `one` compiled while the interpreter and CPython raise `KeyError`, and `1 in {"a"}` was True. That is the latent note at the end of the ADR 0189 entry above, collected. A slot is now the pair everywhere: `d[k] = v` writes key tag *and* value tag with the payloads (`rt_dict_put_tagged`), membership and lookup compare both (`rt_dict_find`, `rt_dict_get_tagged` + `rt_dict_value_tag`, `rt_dict_has_tagged`, `rt_set_contains_tagged`, `rt_contains_tagged`, and `rt_mixed_eq` for `if x == "a":` on a tagged loop variable), `rt_set_discard_tagged` shifts tags with payloads, and a mixed container announces itself with a new `@estr` bit 8 ("the slots describe themselves") so `rt_dict_print`/`rt_set_print` dispatch to the mixed printers while uniform containers keep their static paths untouched. `for k in d` / `for x in s` bind `%_k`/`%_k_tag` exactly as ADR 0185's list loop does; `print(d[k])` and `v = d[k]` fetch the value's tag at the read site. **Lookups compare tags whenever the needle's kind is provable, uniform container or not** — bit 8 is not the gate, because the wrong answer was happening to containers that never mix. Growth stopped being a refusal too: `xs.append("a")` on a list of numbers, `s.add("a")` on a set of numbers, and `d["b"] = "x"` on an int-valued dict now *promote* the container (available only because ADR 0189 made every builder write tags). The dict case had been answering `{'a': 'x', 'b': 'x'}` for `{"a": 1}` + `d["b"] = "x"`, because item assignment overwrote the container's recorded kind and the print followed it; likewise `xs = [1, 2]; xs[0] = "s"` printed `['s', 'b']` — the untouched 2 rendered as whatever string its index names. Both are pinned by parity rows now, AOT ≡ interpreter ≡ CPython, and the two `string_containers_test.go` "must be refused" rows for growth were inverted (ADR 0230's lesson, applied again). Two refusals were added where an answer would have been a guess, both new to this cycle: an element whose kind cannot be proven — `def pick(c): return "z" / return 7`, which printed `(null)` for the 7 because `print` asks at print time and a *slot* is labelled once — and a needle whose kind cannot be proven against a container that mixes. Bools inside containers are accepted and tagged `TagInt`, matching what both backends store today; when L11.2 gives bool its own kind, one line of `elemKindTag` changes and containers follow.<br>↳ ✅ **Done (ADR 0259): a container slot may say `bool` — Gap R.112.** That promise is kept: `elemKindTag` answers `TagBool`, `slotTagSelfDescribing` includes it, and `print([True, 1])` is `[True, 1]`, `print({"k": True})` is `{'k': True}`, `print({True, 1})` is `{True}`, `[x for x in [True, 1, 1]]` is `[True, 1, 1]` — with `[True] == [1]`, `1 in {True}`, `d[True]`, `{True, 1}`-dedup-to-one, `sum([True, 1])` and `True + 1` keeping CPython's numeric answers, because `rt_payload_eq`'s numeric family is int, float **and** bool and the interpreter unboxes a verdict box at every numeric, ordering, equality, membership and `sum` entry. Three things the one-line promise had not counted. (1) Three predicates — `taggableMixedList`, `taggableMixedSet`, `taggableMixedDict` — each restated which tags need the tagged build path, and bool fell through the gap between them, which is why two of the six shapes were **refusals** (“either strings or numbers, not both”, “set literal elements must be constant integers”) rather than wrong answers; all three now ask the tag table through one `elemsTaggable`, and a table test asserts they agree. (2) `value()`'s literal gates asked only `literalNeedsHeap` — “does a payload not fit an `i32`?” — and a bool's fits perfectly, which is precisely why the static global is the wrong place for one; they ask `literalNeedsHeap(n) \|\| g.literalNeedsTags(n)` now, and the same reasoning un-broke a float-holding literal in an argument position (`def half(xs): return xs[0] / 2` / `print(half([1.5]))` answers `0.75`). (3) Tagging `[True, 1]` took `xs[i] + 1` — a program that answered `2` — one step from a refusal, so `numericSlotUse` is the second numeric door: literal-backed container, every slot int-or-bool, the payload is the number whatever the index is. The interpreter mirrors the compiled shape rather than shortcutting it: a verdict in a slot is a boxed `kind:"bool"` object (the float box's shape, not a parallel `[]bool` that every mutation has to shift), `objKindTag("bool")` returns `TagBool`, and the collector's reclaim list knows the kind — one table, both heaps (ADR 0182). And the ordering sentence that ADR 0232 wrote 'int' for now reads `'bool'` on both engines. New unit file `pkg/lang/mixed_dict_set_test.go`, new integration file `integration/mixed_container_test.go` (parity + oracle + refusal + verifier rows).<br>↳ 🟢 **Remaining**, in order: (1a) ~~the other element-wise *reads*~~ — done (ADR 0187); the next element-wise uses need tagged values at the *use* site, which is L11.2; (1b) ~~mixed *dicts* and *sets*~~ — done (ADR 0232), including the tagged lookup ADR 0189 left as a latent note; (1c) floats in containers, which needs a float branch in `rt_print_mixed_value` — the tag exists, the renderer does not; (1d) retiring `@estr[h]` entirely once every read path is tagged; (2) ~~**bools as values**~~ — done in two halves: the print rule by ADR 0257 (`--json` reports `"type": "bool"`, `print(True)` prints `True`) and the **element tag** by ADR 0259 (Gap R.112: a verdict stored in a container slot carries `TagBool`, so the container printer, the set dedup and the ordering sentence all read `bool`); **the operator that chooses an operand, paid by ADR 0261** (Gap R.117: `min`/`max` ask the *chosen* candidate what it is, so `print(max([True, 0]))` is `True`, `max([True, 1])` is `True` and `max([1, True])` is `1` on both engines — one candidate rule and one winner, with `print`/`str()`/`repr()`/f-strings/container tags/`--json` all following the one predicate); **a verdict crossing a call boundary, paid by ADR 0348** (Gap R.111 closed: the call sites answer whether a parameter holds a verdict and the print road asks the front end about the name a call bound — with no boxed verdict, no tag word beside an argument and an IR row that fails if one appears), leaving what that reading will not guess about (Gap R.270: a contradicted position, a method name two classes share) and the residuals ADR 0259 and ADR 0261 filed (Gaps R.116, R.119, R.124, R.125); (3) the `i32 @.strN` / `ret i32 @.str1` / `rt_append(i32, i32 @.lstN)` invalid-IR family (Gap J.6) disappears once elements are tagged, at which point `runtime_ir_test.go` should assert module-wide that no handle constant appears in a value position; Found because `programs/typealias.gy` opens with `type Count = int` — PEP 695, unparseable by Ubuntu 22.04's Python 3.10 — so CI reported oracle drift on a compiler row while the compiler was right. An expectation copied from an external tool is a **versioned dependency of the test suite**: recording the version is worth nothing until a check reads it.<br>↳ **Machine path** — matrix `schema_version` 1.1 adds `python_stdout`/`python_ok`/ `python_error`, `interp_matches_python`/`aot_matches_python`, `oracle` with its `oracle_declared` counterpart, `oracle_reason`/`oracle_ref`/`oracle_rules`/`oracle_notes`/ `oracle_drift`, the `rows`/`skipped` and oracle counters, and a `toolchain` block naming the interpreter and LLVM that produced the artifact. `--schema` gains `definitions.oracleReport` and `definitions.conformanceRow`. `gustyc --oracle <src>` / `--oracle-file <path>` is the ad-hoc form (`--json` for the leg-by-leg report), with **two new exit codes: 6** (gusty disagreed with Python) and **7** (the oracle could not judge the source) — neither may collapse into 1 or 3. `tools/oracleprobe` prints the three legs, so a ledger row is written from measured data rather than memory.<br>↳ **Measured result** — 59 rows: 43 parity cases (still 43/43) + 16 probes; oracle 27 `match` / 22 `debt` / 10 `not_applicable`. **Seven of the rows that used to pass print something other than what CPython prints** (`features_a`, `print_args`, `container_methods`, `none_values`, `string_containers`, `string_escapes`, `string_params`) and eight more are gusty-only surface the oracle cannot run — fifteen cases whose state was previously unrecorded, all now declared, owned and pinned.<br>↳ **Found on its first run**, and in no roadmap row before this: **Gap L.5, `print` is not atomic** (below). `docs/language.md` § print had described the wrong behaviour as intentional ("keeps its place in the line, and both backends interleave it identically") and now states what is actually true.<br>↳ Kept honest by tests, not prose: `pkg/lang/oracle_test.go` (classification, the set rule, and every drift shape including "a leg that used to fail now runs"), `integration/oracle_test.go` (the ledger describes only registered cases, every exception carries reason + owner + pins for both legs, the third leg is not a stub, and **a stubbed pin must produce drift** — the harness is tested against its own ability to fail), and `cmd/gustyc/oracle_test.go` plus the extended `TestCLIExitCodeContract` for the payload and the two new codes. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l11-9) |

(`Gap L.5` and `Gap L.6` were found by this phase's oracle leg and live in the
[Gap L table](#gap-l--values-and-rendering), so they are not repeated here.)

**Machine path (AGENTS.md, non-negotiable).** The tag enum is published as `gustyc --schema`
→ `definitions.valueTag` and named in `--lang`; every refusal carries a stable
`Diagnostic.Code` and appears in `--json`; the exit-code table in `docs/operations.md` is the
implementation for both legs.

### Phase 12 — the Python-visible surface contract

**Goal: a program that reads like Python either runs like Python, or is refused by name.**
Phase 11 settles what a *value* is; Phase 12 settles what the *language says*. They are
separate decisions that meet in the same files, and eight of the thirteen items below are
representation-shaped (they are silently wrong for the reason Phase 11 names). They stay one
phase anyway, because the survey that found them is about the surface, and because a reader
deciding "can I write this program?" needs one table, not two.

The modern-language argument for doing this in 2026 is not "be Python". It is that a
dynamic language is judged by the programs people write without reading a manual, and every
construct in this file's survey was found by writing such a program and being answered a
number nobody wrote. So the phase's contract is a **three-state rule**, and the rule is the
deliverable:

> Every construct is in exactly one of three states — **implemented** on the compiled backend and
> CPython-equal, **refused** by a stable `Diagnostic.Code` with its documented exit class, or
> **absent** from the surface manifest. There is no fourth state. A construct that runs and
> disagrees with CPython is a defect by definition; a construct that parses but no engine
> implements is a front-end error with a span, not a `NameError` three layers from the line
> that meant something.

Three corollaries, each of which is an item below and each of which mirrors a rule this loop
already enforces elsewhere. The rule itself is **[ADR 0233](docs/adr/0233-every-construct-is-implemented-refused-or-absent-never-answer-wrong.md)**;
each item still owes its own ADR before it can be called done.

• **A keyword that is not a keyword is a bug.** `assert`, `del`, `nonlocal` and (per Gap
  R.48) `global` are in nobody's keyword table, so they lex as identifiers: `--check` says
  `undefined name "assert"`, `--file` pays a runtime `NameError` with exit 3, and CPython
  runs the program. One table must drive the lexer, the statement dispatcher, the checker and
  the record, the way `predeclared.go` already drives built-ins (ADR 0166).

• **Protocols are the extension points, and the protocol table is one list.** `__str__` /
  `__repr__` do not reach `print`; `__iter__` / `__next__` hang the record and are
  ignored by the compiler; `__eq__` answers `1` where Python answers `True`; `__property`-style
  descriptors hand back a method object; class bodies bind no attributes at all, which is why
  there is no `Enum`. A class that cannot answer `str(self)` is not an object, and a `for`
  loop that does not read `StopIteration` is not an iterator.

• **Numbers and strings are what the docs say they are.** `int` overflows in silence — and the
  two backends overflow *differently*, so parity cannot see it — and f-string conversions and
  format specs are parsed away, so `f"{3.5:.2f}"` is `3.5`. A bounded integer is a defensible
  2026 design (it is what most compiled dynamic languages ship); a silently wrapping one is
  not.

**The survey (2026-10-01, three engines, one table).** 76 programs, each through `--interp`,
`--aot` and CPython 3.12.3 on the same source; classified by the verdicts, not by intention
(how to re-run it is in the [record](docs/roadmap-details.md#phase-12)):

| State on both legs | Programs | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| CPython-equal on the compiled backend | 9 | the surface that genuinely ships |
| Absent — both legs refuse, CPython runs | 37 | honest absences, mostly this phase's items |
| Refused by the compiled backend only | 16 | the record agrees with Python; codegen declines — 5 of them emit a module `llc` **rejects** (exit 2), which is the fourth state sneaking back in |
| **Runs everywhere, answers wrong** | **8** | the state the language must not have |
| Loops forever / iterates nothing | 2 | `for` over a class with `__iter__` / `__next__` |

`for/else`, `yield from`, f-string interpolation, `print(sep=, end=)`, `sorted(key=, reverse=)`,
`str.split/join/strip/upper/startswith/replace/isdigit/index/count`, dict `keys/values/items/get`,
`in`/`not in`, `is`, ternaries, walrus, list/dict/set comprehensions and `with` were checked and
behave — `with` on both backends, which is also why Gap R.65's stale manifest matters: `--lang`
does not list it.

**Machine path (AGENTS.md, non-negotiable).** The manifest *is* the machine interface: L12.13
publishes the survey's verdicts as data (`gustyc --lang --json` → per construct, per backend,
`supported` / `refused(code)` / `absent`), so an agent plans a program against the language that
exists instead of guessing from a README, and so a construct that ships without being listed
fails a test rather than surprising a user. Every refusal this phase adds carries a
`Diagnostic.Code` from the table in `docs/operations.md`, and every trap carries the exception
class CPython uses (ADR 0212's rule), because `except TypeError:` is part of the surface too.

| ID | Item | Status | Path | ADR | Evidence | Free text (written with the row — the Status column is the authority) | Record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L12.1 | Comparison chains (`a < b < c`) evaluate like Python: one comparison per operator, each middle operand once | ✅ `DONE` — closed by ADR 0288 on 2026-07-06: a comparison node carrying n operands and n−1 operators, at the AST (not an `and` desugaring, which would run a middle call twice); each operand stored once into a local slot and read back by both neighbours, so `print(1 < g() < 10)` runs `g` exactly once on both engines | both | — | `programs/probe_comparison_chains.gy` (six lines; the pre-cycle binary got **four** wrong at exit 0 on both engines), `pkg/lang/compare_chain_test.go` (24 rows × both engines pinned against `python3`, a middle-operand-run-once counter, one-node/`BinOp`-stays-a-`BinOp` shape rows, the `and` boundary, and the container-operand refusal) and `integration/compare_chain_test.go` | Comparison chains mean what they say (OPEN, both backends)<br>`a < b < c` is parsed as `(a < b) < c`, so the middle operand is compared against a boolean. Measured: `x = 5` with `if 1 < x < 3:` takes the branch on **both** backends (CPython does not), and `print(10 < x < 20)` answers `1` where Python answers `False`. `1 < 2 < 3` is right by accident, which is the worst way to be right. Fix in the parser/AST so the checker sees the same shape, and let the middle operand be evaluated once — that is also what makes it cheap: two comparisons, one shared operand, no `and` shortcut that re-evaluates. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l12-1) |

The *str* question (`print`, `str()`, an f-string field, `!s`) asks `__str__`, then `__repr__` the way `object.__str__` does, then the identity form; the *repr* question (`repr()`, every container element, `!r`) asks `__repr__` and nothing else, then the identity form. Both find the dunder through **ADR 0446**'s resolution order and both are keyed by the class id the instance itself carries (`@rt_inst_get(h, 0)`), so a value the expression cannot name still renders as its class says: `print(C())` is `S`, `print([C()])` is `[R]`, `print({C(): 1})` is `{C: 1}`, `print(f"v={x}")` is `v=S`, `str(C())`/`repr(C())` answer instead of refusing. A row is installed only on a PROOF the body hands back a text; a body the compiler can read and that hands back a number installs a row that RAISES `TypeError: __str__ returned non-string (type int)` at the reference's exit class, and a body it cannot read keeps the identity form rather than inventing an answer. The residue the sweep found is filed as **Gap R.508**, **Gap R.509**, **Gap R.510** | both | — | measured on three engines (record) | print ignores `__str__` / `__repr__` (OPEN)<br>`class C: def __str__(self): return "S" / def __repr__(self): return "R"` then `print(C())`: CPython prints `S`, the interpreter prints `<instance>`, the compiled backend prints **`0`** — the interned-index-of-nothing rendered with `%d`, the Gap R.22 signature in a new place. `repr(C())` is not a builtin at all (`NameError`), so the idiom that a debugger, a traceback and every container's `str()` depend on does not exist. `__str__` *is* called by nothing, which is how both backends can be confidently wrong. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l12-3) |

Second, and rarer in the other direction: `class C(A, B)` resolves `a()` but not `b()` in the interpreter (`AttributeError: 'C' has no attribute 'b'`) while the compiled backend resolves both. The fix is one descriptor table — name → how to bind, how to call, how to lower — read by the checker, the interpreter and codegen, so `@property` cannot silently mean "nothing". | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l12-5) |

No trap, no diagnostic, no overflow flag. A bounded `int` is a legitimate 2026 decision (many compiled dynamic languages ship one) *if it is written down and it traps*; silently wrapping is neither design nor accident, it is a bug with a documentation gap attached. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l12-12) |
| L12.13 | The surface manifest is generated from the implementation and published as data (`--lang`, `--schema`) | 🟨 `PARTIAL` — owns Gap R.65 | tooling | — | `gustyc --lang` (ships, hand-written), `gustyc --lang --json` (owed) | The manifest under-reports what ships (PARTIAL)<br>`gustyc --lang` exists and is honest in direction but stale in content: its statement list is `assign, print, if/elif/else, while, for-in-range, def/return, pass, match, try/except/finally, raise, class, import`, which omits `with` (shipped, both backends, documented), `async def`, `yield`, `yield from`, `break`, `continue`; its expression list omits `in`, `is`, `**`, the ternary, the walrus and f-strings, all of which run today. For a toolchain whose second audience is an agent, that is not cosmetic: the manifest is what an agent compiles against, and a stale one sends an agent to plan against a language that does not exist. Generate it from the tables the lexer/parser/checker/codegen already consult (the single-source-of-truth rule of `predeclared.go` / `exceptions.go`), per construct per backend, and let the three-engine census be the thing that checks it. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#l12-13) |

Pinned by `pkg/lang/class_pattern_test.go` (front-end table incl. a cycle, presence/ordering, the two exit-2 shapes as verifying modules, two regex guards over sets of programs) and conformance row 103 `programs/match_classpat.gy` — the first whole-program run this construct ever got. `gustyc --lang` gained the `patterns:` line, without which no agent could discover that class patterns exist at all. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#gap-b) |

A whole-module inference (`pkg/lang/heapargs.go`) now types each parameter as list/dict/set from its annotation, its default, or any call site — propagated to a fixed point so forwarding calls (`def doubled(xs): return total(xs)`) work — and the body uses `rt_list_len`/`rt_get_elem`/`rt_dict_get` accordingly. The runtime now keeps an **interned string table**: `rt_str_intern2(text, repr) -> i32` appends distinct texts to `@str_tab` by `strcmp` (content-addressed, so two separate `"k"` literals are the same dict key) with the Python repr form in the parallel `@str_repr_tab`; container slots hold the index. `rt_print_value(v, isStr, quote)` picks the slot by context, so `print(x)` prints raw text and `print(xs)` prints `['a', 'b']` — and `rt_print_list_str` / `rt_set_print_str` / `rt_dict_print_s` all share that one helper, which is why list, set and dict rendering cannot drift apart.<br>↳ Element kinds are tracked per container and per dict side — `listElemStr`, `setElemStr`, `dictKeyStr`, `dictValStr` — saved and restored in `beginScope`, so `{'ada': 3}` and `{1: 'one'}` both render correctly and one function's `xs` never describes another's.<br>↳ `heapElemKind(b, e)` is the single place a container word is produced (folded int passes through, string interns, anything else is the ADR 0166 diagnostic); every store site goes through it — append, add, setitem, list/dict literal, dict read by key, and the `in` needle, which was the last shape still emitting `rt_contains(i32 %h, i32 @.strN)`.<br>↳ Working and byte-identical in both backends, checked against CPython: string list literal with `len`/index/iteration/`in`, `append`, `xs[0] = "s"`, `s.add`, `d["k"] = v`, `d[1] = "v"`, dict reads by string key, string lists passed to functions, and Python's repr rules (`set()`, `["it's", 'plain']` — single quotes unless the text has `'` and no `"`).<br>↳ The interpreter's `Repr` was fixed alongside: container elements route through `reprNested`, and dict keys print via `Repr` — `%v` used to print the heap handle (`{1048581: 1}` for `{'k': 1}`).<br>↳ Covered by `integration/string_containers_test.go` (20 shapes × both backends × CPython's output), `pkg/lang/string_containers_test.go` (IR invariants: interned store, no `i32 @.str` anywhere, repr table emitted, quote rule) and the new conformance program `string_containers.gy`. `TestIntContainersStillBuild` keeps the guard from becoming a blanket refusal. Remaining, deliberately: an element whose string comes from a `str`-typed **parameter** has no compile-time text to intern and still reports the ADR 0166 diagnostic. Note: `Callable` parameters called through the parameter (`def apply(f, x): return f(x)`) are likewise unsupported in AOT (`codegen: unsupported call "f"`) — the L6.6 Callable surface is therefore checker-only for now. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#gap-i-2) |
| Gap I.3 | Assigned containers are heap handles: folded comprehensions materialise, module definitions allocate + root their slot, per-body binding scope, sorted fixed-point merge | ✅ `DONE` | aot | 0163 | `folded_lists_test.go`, `folded_lists.gy` | assigned containers are heap handles (AOT) — ✅ DONE (ADR 0163). The same class of bug at the *binding* site, all three surfaced by the L8.2 module verifier: assigning a constant-folded comprehension emitted `store i32 @.lst1, i32* %_ys` (rejected by LLVM) and printed an address; module-level `xs = []` left the variable without a slot, so `xs.append(i)` referenced an undefined `%_xs` and `rt_gc` could not see the handle; and `funcDef`'s per-body state leaked into `main`, letting a parameter's alloca be reused by module code. Assignments now materialise folded lists (`rt_alloc`/`rt_set_elem`), module definitions allocate + root their slot, module code starts a fresh binding scope, and the parameter-kind fixed point merges in sorted order (determinism). Covered by `programs/folded_lists.gy` plus unit/integration cases. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#gap-i-3) |

Two bugs, one of them predating the AOT report entirely:<br>↳ **the parser never gave `raise` a span**, so every traceback — interpreter included — said `File "prog", line 0`. `RaiseStmt` now carries the `raise` keyword's position.<br>↳ the compiled report printed no frame at all. Raise sites now emit a pre-rendered frame into a new `@exn_frame` global (` File "prog", line 3, in boom`) and `rt_die` prints it under the header, so the AOT's innermost frame matches the interpreter's. Found on the way: **`strConst` did not escape `"`**, so a double quote in any program string ended the LLVM literal early and the module failed to verify with a nonsense array length ("got type '[7 x i8]' but expected '[31 x i8]'") — a traceback frame, which contains quotes, was the first thing to trip it. Quotes are now `\22` (tabs/CR too). Still open: the AOT report shows only the raise site's own frame, where the interpreter prints one frame per stack level. Its prerequisite has since landed — L8.5 put a real line table in the module (ADR 0231), so the frames an unwinder could read are there; what is missing is the runtime half, an explicit frame stack pushed at each call site to walk. ↳ ✅ **Paid (ADR 0354)** — the artifact was read before the answer was invented, and it said the record has no frames at all (a scan of `testdata/interpreter-golden.json` for `File \"prog\"` returns nothing: a trap is stored as repr, stdout, class and message), so the reference leg is this row\u0027s only witness and CPython is its definition. What shipped is the runtime half and one pass to fill it: `pkg/lang/frame_stack.go` carries the shadow stack (two parallel 64-slot tables, a depth, a snapshot the report prints from, a digits helper so the raise block stays free of `printf`) and `attachFrameStack` lays it over the assembled module, putting a push before every call to a program function — the callee\u0027s name and the caller\u0027s line in one store — and a pop after it; the raise records its own line (`rt_frame_here`, fed by ADR 0171\u0027s span) and copies the stack, because by the time `rt_die` runs every frame has returned. A pass rather than a hunt through the eleven roads that call program code, and gated on `raiseUsed` (set by `setExn`, the one door every raise goes through), so a program that can never report a trap ships the module it always shipped, IR line numbers included. Four things the witnesses decided rather than the plan: the pass also owns the *offsets* it broke (ADR 0231 resolves every `!dbg` against byte positions, so it hands its marks back shifted — a forgotten shift misattributes every statement after the first call and no verifier sees it); a method\u0027s frame says `bump` and not `Counter.bump`, because CPython says `in bump` and the qualified name is the `DISubprogram`\u0027s; a run of identical frames is printed three times and counted, `[Previous line repeated N more times]`, the reference\u0027s own collapse; and the 64-frame table is a *window* — the first cut clamped at slot 63, which left the deepest frames with line 0 and the printer skips an unknown line, quietly reporting a recursion one frame short of the truth. `--json` grows a `frames` member beside `traceback`, produced by `ParseTrapFrames` reading the target\u0027s bytes back so prose and data cannot tell two stories (ADR 0214\u0027s rule, extended from the class to the stack), shaped by `definitions.trapFrames`. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#gap-k-8) |

Fixed at three levels:<br>↳ the checker analyses the arguments of `print` / `len` / `range` (including `sep=`/`end=`), so `error at 1:7: undefined name "undefined_thing"` is a front-end error and exit **1**;<br>↳ **one** built-in name table (`pkg/lang/predeclared.go`) is now predeclared by the checker, consulted by the codegen guard and used for LSP completion — `sum`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `round` and friends had worked in both backends while being unknown to the checker, which is why `print(sum(xs))` failed to compile;<br>↳ codegen refuses a name it has no binding for with an actionable diagnostic instead of a dangling load (ADR 0166). The guard immediately found three bindings that allocated a slot without registering it (`with … as m:` among them). `type` is a reserved word, so `type(x)` is not a call here; it is gone from the built-in table and from LSP completions, which used to suggest source that would not parse. Tests: `TestUndefinedNameInBuiltinCallIsAFrontEndError`, `TestUndefinedNameBuildIsADiagnosticNotAnInvalidModule`, `TestBuiltinsArePredeclaredInTheChecker`, `TestPredeclaredTableCoversTheLSPList`, `TestWithAsTargetIsBound`, `TestCLIBuildTypoIsACompileErrorNotACompilerBug`. `print(undefined_thing)` at module level passes the checker (its arguments are not analysed), codegen emits a reference to the non-existent slot `%_undefined_thing`, and LLVM's verifier rejects the module — so the user is told (correctly, by the contract) that this is a *compiler bug* (exit 2) when they wrote an ordinary typo. `x = undefined_thing` is caught properly, which localises the hole to the print argument path. Fix by analysing print's arguments in the checker, and (per ADR 0166) making codegen refuse an unbound name with an actionable diagnostic instead of emitting a dangling slot. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#gap-k-10) |

L11.9 landed first (ADR 0186) — it is the harness that proves the rest, and from here each item below arrives with a pinned program that has to start printing Python's answer. | [→](docs/roadmap-details.md#gap-l-6) |

The usage line advertises `gustyc [flags] [<src>]` and `docs/operations.md` called `--file` "alias for a positional source", but no branch in `run()` read a positional argument: the command printed the usage banner and exited **0** without compiling anything.
